blocks.text: Wrap a request in an object so it can be queued, logged, retried, or undone.

A **command** turns an operation into data: it carries its receiver and arguments, and exposes `execute()` (and sometimes `undo()`). The **invoker** runs commands without knowing what they do, so it can schedule, record or reverse them. The **receiver** does the real work.

items: **Decouples:** who asks for an action from who performs it, and when.
**Enables:** undo/redo, queues, retries, audit logs, macros.
**Requires:** commands capture what they need to undo themselves.

blocks.text: If you only need to run something later, a lambda or `Runnable` is already a command. The pattern pays off once you add undo, persistence or logging.

walkthrough.note: The receiver is plain state with no knowledge of commands. Commands are the only ones who modify it here.
The command contract: do it, and reverse it. Invokers depend on nothing else.
`Insert` is reversible from its own fields. `Delete` captures the removed text during `execute`, because undo cannot recompute what is gone.
The invoker runs a command and keeps it on a stack. It never inspects the command type, so history and undo work for any command.
Three edits, then two undos walk back through history in reverse order: delete, then the second insert.

blocks.text: An order service enqueues `SendInvoice(orderId)` and `ResizeImage(assetId, width)` as small serializable records in a database table. Workers on other machines load a row, run it, and mark it done. Failures retry with backoff, an admin screen lists and cancels pending jobs, and the same table is the audit log. The web request returns before any work happens.

lines: sealed interface Job permits SendInvoice, ResizeImage {}

blocks.text: Payoff: work becomes data. It can wait, move between machines, be retried and be inspected, with no change to the code that requested it.

lists.title: Use when
items: Operations need undo/redo, history or an audit trail.
Work must be queued, scheduled, retried or sent to another process.
Operations should be composable into macros or batches.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: A direct call or a one-shot callback is enough.
Undo cannot be defined, for instance after an irreversible side effect.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Undo that does not capture prior state, such as the deleted text.
Commands holding live references that change before they run.
Retries need idempotent commands; otherwise they run twice.
Serialized commands need versioning when their shape changes.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: A command class per button that only forwards one call.
Unbounded history that keeps every object alive.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Lambdas and `Runnable` are commands without undo.
Sealed interfaces of records make serializable, exhaustively handled commands.

rows.difference: A strategy answers how to do one job right now. A command packages a request to run, queue or undo later.
Undo can restore a snapshot (memento) instead of computing an inverse. Heavy edits favor snapshots; small ones favor inverse operations.
A macro command is a composite: it holds a list of commands and executes or undoes them as one.
Commands travel down a handler chain so that one handler can validate, log or reject them.
A saga is a long-running sequence of commands where each step has a compensating command.

template: class Doc { final StringBuilder text = new StringBuilder(); }
interface Command { void execute(); void undo(); }
record Insert(Doc d, int at, String s) implements Command { public void execute() { d.text.insert(at, s); } public void undo() { d.text.delete(at, at + s.length()); } }
class History { void run(Command c) { c.execute(); } void undo() {} }

exercises.prompt: Explain Command in your own words: what does packaging a request as an object buy you, and what must a command capture to be undoable?

modelAnswer.text: Command turns an operation into an object with its receiver and arguments. An invoker can then run it later, queue it, log it, retry it or send it elsewhere without knowing what it does. For undo, a command must capture whatever it needs to reverse itself, such as the deleted text, while executing. Strategy differs: it picks how to do a job now.

keyPoints: Request becomes an object: receiver plus arguments
Invoker is decoupled from what the command does
Enables queue, log, retry, undo and macros
Undo needs state captured during execute
Strategy chooses how now; command packages what to run later
